files.lesson.md: --- order: 28 unit: proof10 node: AC9M10SP01 n2 uses: [AC9M8SP02 n1, AC9M7M04 n3, AC9M7M05 n3] assumes: [AC9M10SP01 n1] title: Writing a proof summary: "A proof is a list of statements, each with a reason: a given fact, a rule you already know, or an earlier line. Writing one for opposite angles of a parallelogram shows the habit: no line without a reason." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Mia measured four parallelograms and says opposite angles are always equal. Ben asks, \"How do you know the fifth one won't break it?\" What could Mia say that Ben couldn't argue with?" app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8421 url: http://127.0.0.1:8421/index.html readySelector: "#gclass" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: proof.yml#explain-pic, caption: "A parallelogram ABCD. A + B = 180° and B + C = 180°, both co-interior angles, so A = C." } explainClip: query: { code: "@proof.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Each statement has a reason" say: "A proof gives a reason for every statement." clip: - caption: { text: "A + B = 180°: co-interior angles, AD parallel to BC.", say: "A and B add to one eighty. Co-interior angles." } - wait: 1200 - caption: { text: "B + C = 180°: co-interior angles, AB parallel to DC.", say: "B and C add to one eighty too." } - wait: 1200 - caption: { text: "So A = C. Every line has a reason.", say: "So A equals C. Every line has a reason." } - wait: 1200 --- A **proof** is a short list of statements. Each one comes with a reason: something given, a rule you already know, or a line you have already proved. If a line has no reason, a careful reader can say "so what?". ## Predict: the opposite corner ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to the angle at C when A is 70° shows who expects opposite angles to be equal and who thinks the shape's sides decide it. The proof then says why." check: type: predict q: "ABCD is a parallelogram and angle $A = 70^\\circ$. What is angle $C$, the opposite corner?" options: - "$70^\\circ$" - "$110^\\circ$" - "$20^\\circ$" - "$90^\\circ$" actual: "70°. Angle B is 110° (it makes 180° with A), and C makes 180° with B, so C is 70°. That is the reasoning to write down." ``` You have a guess. Now find out how to write down why. ## Run: try parallelograms ```step stage: run insight: "Dragging parallelograms and comparing a and c is a demonstration; the proof then gives the reason that works for all of them." try: { playground: board, starter: "proof.yml#run", height: 640 } check: { type: board, text: "Drag the corners to make a different parallelogram, with angle $a$ more than $90^\\circ$. Compare $a$ and $c$. Was your prediction right? Does that prove it for every parallelogram?", when: "p = 2 and a > 90", explain: "a and c match every time, but only for the parallelograms you made. The proof gives the reason." } ``` The panel names the shape. Keep it a parallelogram: opposite sides parallel. ## Investigate: statements and reasons ```step stage: investigate insight: "A proof lists statements, each with a reason. The reason is a given, a known rule or an earlier line. Nia's mistake uses the conclusion as a reason; the key reason in each chain is the parallel-line rule." tasks: - check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Triangle ABC has interior angles $a$ at A and $b$ at B. The side AC is extended past C to make an exterior angle $x$. Prove that $x = a + b$." steps: - ["$c = 180^\\circ - a - b$", "angles in a triangle add to $180^\\circ$"] - ["$x = 180^\\circ - c$", "$c$ and $x$ are on a straight line, so they add to $180^\\circ$"] - ["$x = 180^\\circ - (180^\\circ - a - b) = a + b$", "put the first line into the second and simplify"] picks: - step: 2 q: "What is the reason for $x = 180^\\circ - c$?" options: ["Angles on a straight line add to 180°", "Angles in a triangle add to 180°", "Alternate angles are equal"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "x is not inside the triangle.", "There are no parallel lines in this triangle."] criteria: - "Every line has a reason after it." - "My reasons are given facts or rules I know, not 'it looks like it'." - "My last line is what I was asked to prove." explain: "c = 180° − a − b (triangle), x = 180° − c (straight line), so x = a + b. Each statement has a reason. This works for every triangle, because a and b stand for any angles." smaller: check: type: question q: "Just the first line. Which first statement, with its reason, starts the proof?" options: ["$c = 180^\\circ - a - b$, because angles in a triangle add to $180^\\circ$", "$x = a + b$, because it looks the same", "$c = x$, because they are next to each other"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is what we want to prove, so it cannot be a reason.", "c and x are on a straight line: they add to 180°, they are not equal."] explain: "Start with what you know: the three angles of the triangle add to 180°, so c = 180° − a − b." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#nia" text: "Nia tries to prove that opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal. Click the line where her reasoning goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: proof-assumes-conclusion explain: "Line 3: \"opposite angles are equal\" is exactly what Nia is meant to prove. A reason cannot be the conclusion. She needs a different reason, such as co-interior angles at the parallel sides." - check: type: question q: "In parallelogram ABCD, $AD \\parallel BC$. What is the reason for \"angle $A$ + angle $B$ = $180^\\circ$\"?" options: ["Co-interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°", "Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal", "Angles in a quadrilateral add to 360°", "They look like they do"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Alternate angles are equal, they do not add to 180°. A and B are on the same side of AB.", "That is true, but it does not give A + B on its own. Two angles would be unknown.", "A reason has to be a fact or a rule."] explain: "A and B are between the parallel lines AD and BC, on the same side of the transversal AB. That makes them co-interior, so they add to 180°." ``` ### Prove it, line by line Here is a proof that opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal. Each line says what is true and why. ```worked ABCD \text{ is a parallelogram}, \text{ so } AD \parallel BC \text{ and } AB \parallel DC :: Given. This is what a parallelogram is. \angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ :: Co-interior angles, $AD \parallel BC$. \angle B + \angle C = 180^\circ :: Co-interior angles, $AB \parallel DC$. \angle A = 180^\circ - \angle B = \angle C :: Both $A$ and $C$ equal $180^\circ - \angle B$, so $\angle A = \angle C$. ``` The two parallel pairs are the only facts it needed, so it holds for every parallelogram: a rectangle, a rhombus, any slant. Now try one on paper with the example beside you. Prove that an exterior angle of a triangle equals the two interior angles opposite it. Write each line with its reason, then pick the reason that matters. ### Find the mistake Read Nia's working. Is her last line a reason, or the thing she is proving? ### Pick the reason Look at where A and B sit between the parallel sides. ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: the same proof for a rectangle, a sum from one line of the proof, and a shape where a missing parallel pair breaks it." try: { playground: board, starter: "proof.yml#trapezium", height: 640 } tasks: - check: type: question q: "Does the same proof show that opposite angles of a rectangle are equal?" options: ["Yes: a rectangle is a parallelogram, so every step still holds", "No: a rectangle needs its own proof", "Only if the rectangle is a square", "No: rectangles have right angles, so they are not parallelograms"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The proof used only the two pairs of parallel sides. A rectangle has them.", "It holds for every rectangle, not only squares.", "A rectangle is a parallelogram with right angles."] explain: "The proof used only AD ∥ BC and AB ∥ DC. A rectangle (and a rhombus, and a square) has both, so it is covered." - check: { type: number, q: "In parallelogram ABCD, angle $A = 65^\\circ$. Use the proof's second line to find angle $B$, in degrees.", answer: 115, explain: "A + B = 180° (co-interior angles), so B = 180 − 65 = 115°." } - hint: ["Make a quadrilateral with only one pair of parallel sides.", "Compare a and c."] check: { type: board, text: "Edge case: a trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides. Drag the corners so $p = 1$ and look at $a$ and $c$. Does the proof still show $a = c$?", when: "p = 1 and a > 100", explain: "a and c are no longer equal: the proof needs both pairs of parallel sides, and a trapezium has only one." } ``` ### A rectangle ### Using one line ### One pair of parallel sides ## Practise: reasons ```step stage: practise insight: "Choosing the reason, using the proof's lines to find angles, and a review of the exterior angle shortcut." tasks: - check: type: question q: "In parallelogram ABCD, $AB \\parallel DC$. What is the reason for \"angle $B$ + angle $C$ = $180^\\circ$\"?" options: ["Co-interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°", "Alternate angles between parallel lines are equal", "Vertically opposite angles are equal", "Angles in a triangle add to 180°"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Alternate angles are equal, they do not add to 180°.", "B and C are not vertically opposite.", "There is no triangle here."] explain: "B and C sit between AB and DC, on the same side of the transversal BC: co-interior." - check: type: number q: "ABCD is a parallelogram. Angle $A = (2x + 10)^\\circ$ and angle $C = (3x - 20)^\\circ$. Find $x$." answer: 30 tolerance: 0 explain: "Opposite angles are equal: 2x + 10 = 3x − 20, so x = 30 (and A = C = 70°)." - check: type: question q: "Which statement can be the first line of a proof that a parallelogram's opposite angles are equal?" options: ["AD ∥ BC and AB ∥ DC, because ABCD is a parallelogram", "A = C, because opposite angles are equal", "A = C, because they look the same", "A = 70°, because I measured it"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That is what you are trying to prove.", "A reason has to be a fact, not a look.", "That is one case."] explain: "Start from what is given: a parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides." - check: { type: number, q: "Review: a triangle has angles $a = 48^\\circ$ and $b = 75^\\circ$. The side through C is extended, making an exterior angle $x$ at C. What is $x$, in degrees?", answer: 123, tolerance: 0, explain: "x = a + b = 48 + 75 = 123°. (c = 57°, and 180 − 57 = 123°.)" } ``` ### Straight to the reason ### Opposite angles ### The first line ### Review: exterior angle ## Make: back to Mia and Ben ```step stage: make insight: "Writing a full proof for the other pair of opposite angles, then saying why Mia's four measurements could not have done it: the reason covers every parallelogram." tasks: - hint: ["Follow the plan: say what is parallel, then use co-interior angles twice.", "This time start from angle B."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Prove that angle $B$ = angle $D$ in parallelogram ABCD. Write each line with its reason. Then pick the reason for the key step." steps: - ["$AD \\parallel BC$ and $AB \\parallel DC$", "ABCD is a parallelogram (given)"] - ["$\\angle B + \\angle C = 180^\\circ$", "co-interior angles, $AB \\parallel DC$"] - ["$\\angle C + \\angle D = 180^\\circ$", "co-interior angles, $AD \\parallel BC$"] - ["$\\angle B = 180^\\circ - \\angle C = \\angle D$", "both equal $180^\\circ - \\angle C$"] picks: - step: 3 q: "What is the reason for angle $C$ + angle $D$ = $180^\\circ$?" options: ["Co-interior angles, because AD ∥ BC", "Alternate angles, because AD ∥ BC", "Angles in a triangle add to 180°"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Alternate angles are equal, they do not add to 180°.", "There is no triangle in this proof."] criteria: - "My first line says what is given." - "Every line has a reason that is a fact or a rule." - "My last line is angle B = angle D, and does not use that fact as a reason." explain: "Given: both pairs of sides parallel. B + C = 180° and C + D = 180° (co-interior angles), so B = D." - check: type: question q: "Why could Mia's four measured parallelograms not do what the proof does?" options: ["Four parallelograms are four cases, and the proof's reason works for every parallelogram", "Her protractor was not accurate enough", "She should have measured more than four", "Parallelograms cannot be measured"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Better measuring improves the cases but does not add the ones not measured.", "Forty parallelograms are still forty cases.", "They can be measured. The measurements are evidence, not a proof."] explain: "Measurements are cases. The proof used only the two pairs of parallel sides, which every parallelogram has." ``` ### Angle B and angle D Write this on paper first, a line at a time with its reason. Then pick the reason for the key step. ### Mia and Ben **Also used in** - **Quadrilaterals.** The Year 8 proofs used congruent triangles. This one uses parallel lines. Both are lists of statements with reasons. - **Everywhere reasons are needed.** A lawyer, a scientist and a programmer each say what is given, what rule they use, and what follows. - **Using theorems.** The next lesson picks the theorem that fits a problem and uses it in a short proof. ```teacher summary: Students write proofs as statements with a reason for each, for opposite angles of a parallelogram and for an exterior angle of a triangle, and learn that a reason cannot be the conclusion (AC9M10SP01, node 2). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 12 min goals: - I can write a proof as statements, each with a reason. - I can use the parallel-line rules and the angle sum as reasons. - I can tell when a line has no reason, or uses the conclusion as its reason. struggle: Writing the reason for every line, and not using the thing to be proved as a reason. After each line ask 'how do you know?' until the answer is a given, a rule or an earlier line. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need co-interior and alternate angles (Parallel lines), the angle sum, and Proving quadrilateral properties from Year 8 for the idea of proof. The one idea: a proof is a list of statements, each with a reason that is a given, a rule or an earlier line. The common mistake is giving the conclusion as the reason (Nia's working). Hinge node: the first line is the one students stick on. The smaller step asks only for that line and its reason. A two-column layout is fine, but any clear layout with reasons works. The proof of B = D mirrors the worked proof of A = C. If students prefer, they can use the triangle proof for the exterior angle in the same layout. Nothing here is a real measurement. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Most will say 70°. Ask them why, and write the first reason they say on the board." - "Run: ask whether any parallelogram will break it. Keep asking what would convince Ben." - "Paper: the exterior angle proof after the worked example and the proof of B = D in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for a reason beside every line." - "Investigate: ask a student to read Nia's line 3 aloud and say what it is being used for." - "Modify: before the trapezium, ask which line of the proof would stop working." - "Make: ask what Ben could still argue with." stuck: - see: A student writes a line with no reason. ask: How do you know that? fix: Write 'because' and finish it with a given, a rule or an earlier line. - see: A student uses the conclusion as a reason (Nia's mistake). ask: Is that the thing you were asked to prove? fix: Go back to what is given (parallel sides) and use a rule such as co-interior angles. - see: A student uses alternate angles for A + B = 180°. ask: Do alternate angles add to 180° or are they equal? fix: "A and B are on the same side of the transversal: co-interior, so they add to 180°." stretch: Prove that adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to 180°, then that a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite angles equal is a parallelogram. support: "A proof frame: 'Given: __. Line 1: __ because __. Line 2: __ because __. So __.' and a picture of the parallelogram with the parallel sides marked." leads: > This covers AC9M10SP01 node 2. Where it leads: Using theorems (next lesson), where a short proof shows a frame is a rectangle, and the proofs students will meet in senior mathematics. exit: q: Triangle ABC has a = 50° and b = 60°. Side AC is extended past C, making an exterior angle x. Write a proof, with a reason for each line, that x = a + b. a: c = 180° − 50° − 60° = 70° (angles in a triangle). x = 180° − 70° = 110° (angles on a straight line). So x = 110° = a + b. explain: > A **proof** is a list of statements, each with a **reason**. A reason is a given fact, a rule you already know (such as co-interior angles add to 180°), or a line you have already proved. To prove opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal: A + B = 180° and B + C = 180° (co-interior angles), so A = C. A reason cannot be the conclusion itself. ```
